stories.title: How much more are you spending on petrol since the war in Iran began?
stories.summary: At least 145 countries have reported increases in petrol prices since the attacks on Iran by the US and Israel began on February 28. Since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran six months ago, petrol prices have risen in at least 145 countries, adding to the burden on consumers worldwide. The figures are based on data from GlobalPetrolPrices, which tracks fuel prices in 170 countries and territories. Petrol prices in Myanmar rose the most, increasing by 56 percent from $0.77 per litre [0.26 gallon} of 95-octane fuel on February 23 to $1.20 on August 17. Bhutan recorded the next-largest increase at 55 percent, followed by Cuba at 51 percent, the UAE at 50 percent and 48 percent in Nigeria. In 25 other countries, most of them oil producers with heavily subsidised fuel, prices have either remained unchanged or fallen by single digits. The table below lists the 145 countries where petrol prices at the pump increased over the past six months. Before the war, the US national average for a gallon [3.78 litres] of regular petrol was $2.94. It now costs $4.09, an increase of 39 percent, according to AAA Fuel Prices, which tracks retail fuel prices for the American Automobile Association (AAA). The extra cost directly affects how far people can travel. Before the war, $50 worth of fuel in the US could take a family sedan roughly 718 km (446 miles). Today, the same amount takes you about 536 km (333 miles) – 183 km less, a 25 percent reduction in driving distance.

stories.title: Almost half the minors recruited by armed groups in 2025 were approached via social media
stories.summary: Some 44% of children and adolescents recruited by armed groups in Colombia during 2025 were approached through social media or platforms such as TikTok and Facebook, according to data from the Special Jurisdiction for Peace cited in a Human Rights Watch report published on Monday.
article_sentences: Some 44% of children and adolescents recruited by armed groups in Colombia during 2025 were approached through social media or platforms such as TikTok and Facebook, according to data from the Special Jurisdiction for Peace cited in a Human Rights Watch report published on Monday.
The 124-page document, titled “I Thought I Would Never See My Mother Again,” draws on 184 interviews with officials, humanitarian workers, indigenous and community leaders and child protection staff.

The organisation analysed records held by the Ombudsman's Office and counted at least 1,500 minors recruited since 2021, with a marked rise from 2023: that year the office documented 342 cases, reaching 625 in 2024, an increase of 81%.

“Armed groups in Colombia are recruiting children with impunity, as protection systems fail and social media becomes a more effective recruitment tool,” said Juanita Goebertus, the organisation's Americas director.

The report states that over the past decade around 1% of recruitment complaints led to a criminal investigation and only 0.2% ended in a conviction, mostly of those who carried out the recruitment rather than those bearing greatest responsibility.
More than half the cases are concentrated in Cauca department, and FARC dissident groups are behind the majority of complaints.
Between 2020 and 2025 those recruited were most often 15 or 16 years old, though more than 30% of cases involved minors aged between 10 and 14.
Child protection officials told the organisation of cases involving children of nine or ten.
Human Rights Watch notes that under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, recruiting children under 15 may constitute a war crime.
Indigenous children account for almost half of documented cases between 2021 and 2025, despite indigenous peoples making up around 4% of Colombia's population.
The proportion of girls, averaging 40%, has risen since 2021.
Once recruited, minors are usually moved far from their home areas to prevent escape and sever family ties.
